# Parallel Rendering

Rendering pages with Quarto takes up most of a build, and Quarto renders them one after another in
a single process. For a package with a large API (a thousand or more reference pages, plus a User
Guide) that can mean builds of half an hour or more. With `--jobs`, Great Docs splits the pages
into groups and renders them with several Quarto processes at once, so the render takes a fraction
of the time.

::: {.callout-warning}
## This feature is experimental

Parallel rendering is off by default and may change in future releases. It is designed to produce
the same site as an ordinary build, and it falls back to rendering in one process for the kinds of
site it knows it can't split. Still, it hasn't yet been tried on as many sites as the ordinary
build. If a parallel build looks different from an ordinary one, please [open an
issue](https://github.com/posit-dev/great-docs/issues).
:::

## Turning It On

Pass `--jobs auto` to let Great Docs choose the number of processes from your CPU count:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
great-docs build --jobs auto
```

Or give a number yourself (`-j` is the short form):

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
great-docs build -j 4
```

To use parallel rendering for every build without changing the command, set the
`GREAT_DOCS_RENDER_JOBS` environment variable. This is handy in CI:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
export GREAT_DOCS_RENDER_JOBS=auto
great-docs build
```

The Python API takes the same values:

```{.python filename="Python"}
from great_docs import GreatDocs

docs = GreatDocs()
docs.build(jobs="auto")
```

With `auto`, Great Docs uses one process per performance core on Apple silicon Macs and one per CPU
elsewhere, up to a maximum of eight. Each process is a full Quarto render with its own memory, so a
smaller number is the safer choice on a machine that's short of memory.

## How Much Faster?

The speedup depends on the number of pages and on how many processes your machine can run at once.
Sites with fewer than 40 pages render in one process, since starting several processes would cost
more time than it saves. In our tests on a laptop with six performance cores:

| Site | Ordinary build | `--jobs auto` |
|------|----------------|---------------|
| 395 pages | 2 min 36 s | 52 s |
| 1,865 pages | 19 min 9 s | 3 min 12 s |

The gain grows with the size of the site. Part of it comes from parallelism, and part from a leaner
Quarto configuration that each process reads. Quarto rereads the configuration for every page, so
trimming it saves more time the more pages there are.

The pages are split using the per-page times from the last build (see
[Build Timings](13-building.qmd#build-timings)), so groups take about the same time each. A second
parallel build is usually a little faster than the first for this reason.

## What You'll See

The build log reports how the pages were split:

```{.default filename="Build log excerpt"}
━━ Step 19/20 ─ Build site with Quarto ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
      Rendering 1865 pages in 33 groups with 6 Quarto processes
   ✔ Site rendered  3m 12.2s
```

When a site can't be split safely, the log says why and the build carries on in one process:

```{.default filename="Build log excerpt"}
      Rendering in one process: only 12 pages
```

Either way, the site is assembled in `docs/_site/` as usual, and the per-page timings and the
[freeze cache](37-freeze.qmd) are saved as after an ordinary build.

## How It Works

Each Quarto process works in its own copy of the build directory, so no two processes ever write to
the same file. Every copy holds the whole project, which means each process sees all of the pages
when it builds the navigation, resolves cross-references, and fills in the search index. A parallel
build goes like this:

1. The pre-render scripts (such as the one that restores the freeze cache) run once.
2. The pages are planned into groups, keeping the pages of a blog listing together.
3. The processes take groups from a shared queue, largest first, until all are rendered.
4. The rendered pages, search index, sitemap, and freeze cache entries from every copy are merged
   into the site.
5. The post-render scripts run once, as after an ordinary render.

If anything unexpected happens along the way (Quarto doesn't render a page it should have, or the
outputs can't be merged), the parallel output is discarded and the site is rendered the ordinary
way.

## Which Builds Use It

Parallel rendering applies to ordinary single-version builds. It is ignored for:

- [multi-version sites](30-multi-version-docs.qmd), which already build their versions in parallel
- `great-docs build --watch`, which uses Quarto's preview server
- `great-docs build --from-repo`, which doesn't take `--jobs` yet

A site also renders in one process when it has fewer than 40 pages, a page with a `listing:` at the
top of the site, a listing that includes pages from outside its own directory, or a file with a
glob character (such as `*` or `[`) in its path.

## Things to Keep in Mind

**Code cells on different pages can run at the same time.** With the default `freeze: auto`, only
pages whose source changed run their code, but those that do may run alongside each other. Each
process has its own copy of the project, so files written with relative paths stay separate. Code
that uses a shared resource (an absolute path, a local database, a fixed network port) could see
two pages at once.

**Pre-render scripts may run twice.** If the parallel render falls back to one process after your
`pre_render` scripts have run, the ordinary render runs them again. Scripts that can safely run
twice (as the built-in freeze restore does) are unaffected.

**The search index and sitemap are in a different order.** Their entries are the same as in an
ordinary build, but in another order, which makes no difference to search or to search engines.

**Windows is untested.** Parallel rendering should work there, but it has so far been used only on
macOS and Linux.

## Checking a Parallel Build

To compare a parallel build with an ordinary one, build the site both ways and diff the results:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
great-docs build && cp -R docs/_site /tmp/site-ordinary
great-docs build --jobs auto
diff -r /tmp/site-ordinary docs/_site
```

Expect `search.json` and `sitemap.xml` to differ in their order only. Any other difference is worth
reporting.
